paragraphs.rawText: [II.1.1] Once Herod was buried, the people freely brought out their judgements, as is usual against the dead: he had been oppressive and intolerable to them; he had exercised unjust rule over his fellow citizens, a tyrant, not a king; a murderer of his own kin at home, a plunderer in public, he had left nothing to anyone. Tribute had been added, everything exhausted, foreigners enriched and Jews emptied of their wealth. He had brought an enemy into the temple and contaminated all its sacred things with sacrilege. Happy were those who had died, since the living never lacked torments. In a few years under Herod’s rule, after their captivity had been cast off, Judaea had endured more evils than it had borne in captivity itself under a barbarian enemy, when the kings of the Babylonians ruled over them. Exile under those kings had been more tolerable than dwelling at home under Herod: those kings had sent them back to their own homes, but he had driven them away. He had been more merciless than Darius, prouder than Artaxerxes, more rapacious than the Medes. They had hoped for an end to their evils, that they might leave exile if he ended his days, but Archelaus had added himself to the misery of their slavery as a self-appointed successor, reproducing Herod and adding new evils. It was a misery in kingdoms that a master was chosen, and a greater misery that he was imposed upon the unwilling. It seemed a consolation in slavery if they chose their own master, since he became kinder if rule was conferred upon him, prouder if he usurped it. Archelaus would therefore be far more intolerable than Herod, since the former had assumed kingship, while the latter had received it.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.1.2] These things were not only discussed frequently in Judaea but also thrown in Archelaus’s face at Rome, as he stood before Caesar and the senate and his accusers pleaded their case. There was a long contest there over confirming or revoking Archelaus’s kingship. When a place had been assigned for the hearing in the temple of Apollo, which Caesar had founded and embellished with many ornaments, Salome’s son Antipater, a powerful speaker, developed the arguments we have given above and many others. He marvelled that Archelaus made a show of seeking kingship from Caesar, when by a reckless usurpation he had long since acted as king in Judaea without consulting Caesar. For what else were the golden chair and the diadem brought before him but the insignia of kingship? With what arrogance had he presumed to sit upon the royal throne? From a lofty seat he greeted the people, surrounded by close ranks of soldiers. The diadem was brought out according to the custom and practice of emperors, although it ought to have been reserved for Caesar’s judgement, both because of the authority of Roman rule and because of the legal force of the will. For Herod could not have forestalled Caesar or the senate in a matter in which he himself had either received authority from the senate or received it back from Caesar. In his earlier will he had expressed a sufficiently clear indication of his own wishes, declaring with sound judgement and considered counsel that Antipas should succeed him in the kingdom. In his later will he had reserved everything for Caesar’s judgement, although his body was already failing and, anxious at his mortal danger and no longer capable of any judgement or counsel, he had dictated what was put before him rather than what he himself thought. The man who had forestalled the grant of rule had therefore pronounced upon himself that he did not deserve to be appointed to the kingdom by your judgement, Caesar; for, had he been conscious of his own merit, he would have hastened to ask rather than to seize. By usurping what depended upon a petition instead of petitioning for it, men commonly prejudiced their case even in financial disputes, so that litigants who reversed the proper order lost their suit. Here, however, the charge concerned no monetary gain: the rights of Roman rule had been violated, its dignity despised, its authority spurned. The senate of the Roman curia, accustomed to give and take away kingdoms, had been judged unworthy to preserve, together with Caesar, its ancient prerogative of conferring rule. What would he, who had grown insolent even before his reign, do once he began to reign lawfully? Very many had also been killed because they had sought relief for their exhausted resources and a lightening of tribute. War had been imposed upon those asking for a remedy; nine thousand Jews had been killed in the very celebration of Passover, revered among their people; human beings had been sacrificed in place of animals; the blood of the consecrated, who had gathered for the temple’s festivals, had been poured out—a pitiable spectacle. Anyone who surveyed the slaughter of the dead would think that the Babylonians had returned. How much more cruel were deeds committed by a fellow citizen that would be judged full of monstrous savagery and impiety even in a barbarian enemy! This was the dole given to the citizens; with this sacrifice Archelaus had commended the beginnings of his kingship. Caesar and the senate ought to pity the remnants of Judaea, once supported by free peoples, which now wished for slavery, if only it could endure a tolerable slavery under a just king. Archelaus was far from possessing the right to rule, since among the Jews kingship belonged to no one except a man descended from Judah, as the law said. But this man, of Idumaean stock, with no connection by birth to the royal line, had crept into an honour not owed to him. Antipater had been grandfather to both the speaker and Archelaus, outstanding in wealth and powerful in other accomplishments, especially in his friendship with the Romans, and proven in war to the elder Caesar. Although he could have claimed kingship for himself, he had never sought it; indeed, he had preferred to defend it for others rather than obtain it for himself. He had deservedly been regarded as the best of fathers, having won freedom for Judaea by his wounds, without bringing it into slavery. Herod had aspired to kingship through the testimony of Antony, his father’s guest-friend. From that time the fortunes of the Jews had declined: Herod had acted as an enemy, not a ruler. Since he himself had been an adulterer of kingship, how could a lawful king have been created by him? They did not, however, plead to be free of kingship, but asked to be under Roman rule, whose favour had already been secured for them in the days of the Maccabees. Through the later usurpation of kingship they had declined so far that they were much inferior to those against whom they had sought alliance with Rome. Finally, he said that they begged, “Grant Judaea government by a provincial governor on the same terms as Syria, so that our devotion may be put to the test: whether we, who are called seditious and rebellious, can obey moderate judges.”

paragraphs.rawText: [II.1.3] Replying to these arguments on Archelaus’s behalf, Nicolaus maintained that a most unruly nation had paid the penalty for its insolence, lest Archelaus should above all incur the odium of an inexcusable crime if they disturbed the peace by sedition and withdrew in mind and arms from alliance with the Romans. On the question of which will should take precedence, he asked who could doubt it, “when a later will is usually preferred to earlier ones, and this one ought to be regarded as much stronger than the rest, since in it Caesar’s prerogative of confirming the royal judgement has been preserved? By this the dignity of the Roman name is increased rather than diminished, if you, Caesar, do not deny kings what private persons are allowed—that their wills should be valid and that in their last writing they should name the person they most wish to succeed them—and if kings in turn preserve this honour for you, that confirmation of their judgement should be sought from you, so that the man whom his father has chosen and you have approved should succeed. When, then, did Herod show greater judgement: when he preserved your prerogative, Caesar, or when he passed you over? Where Antipas is appointed successor, Caesar is passed over; where Archelaus is appointed, Caesar is brought in. Without a foundation nothing is stable. Thus, by divine judgement, where justice was lacking, neither pretence nor intention had a foundation; but where fairness of mind was present, strength was sought to confirm the judgement. Consider, then, whether the man who chose you did you an injury, or whether what he left to be ratified by your arbitration ought to be annulled, when you are lord of all things, to whom even kings rightly yield power. For he who knew whom to choose to confirm his judgement certainly knew whom to choose to rule; nor could he be mistaken in his successor when he was not mistaken in the person who would confirm his judgement. For the man who appointed you arbiter certainly knew that he must appoint a successor whom you would not be displeased to appoint.”

paragraphs.rawText: [II.1.4] After hearing both sides, Caesar deferred his sentence. Then, after consulting the senate, he placed Archelaus over the nation, to discharge the office of ruler without the honour of kingship. He nevertheless promised to grant him kingship too, if he conducted himself so as to win approval. Attempts at revolt among the people of Israel were already being reported. He appointed two of Herod’s sons as tetrarchs, Philip and Antipas, who had contested the kingship with Archelaus. He preserved the bequest to Herod’s sister, whose name was Salome, and himself added other gifts. He also judged that the thousand talents left to him should be divided between Herod’s two daughters, added another six hundred thousand, and decreed that they should be joined in marriage to Pheroras’s children.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.2.1] Meanwhile, a young man pretended to be Alexander, claiming that those whom his father Herod had charged with the killing had taken pity and, substituting others in his place, had released him together with his brother Aristobulus. He made for Miletus and from there for Rome, so that it would be harder to recognise him among strangers.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.2.2] There he would easily have stirred up the Jews, who were most ready for political change, had Caesar not learnt the facts and ordered a certain Celadus, who had known Alexander thoroughly, to bring the man to him at once. When Celadus saw the young man, he hesitated, deceived by the resemblance; but, seeing that the other signs did not agree, he asked where Aristobulus was. The man asserted that he was staying on the island of Cyprus to guard against plots, because it would be easier to kill the brothers if they were together. Then, when he was brought before Caesar, on a promise of impunity he immediately disclosed that, relying upon his resemblance in appearance, he had pretended to be Alexander so as to obtain countless gifts from the Jews as a king’s son. Caesar laughed at the deceit, but let the man himself go unpunished and pronounced those who had given him gifts beyond the measure due to a private person, as though he were a king’s son, sufficiently punished by the immense losses they had borne in unnecessary expenditure.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.2.4] He deservedly paid this price, for he had not restrained his desires even from his own brother’s wife. When Alexander died, delivered to death at his father’s command, his wife Glaphyra, daughter of Archelaus, king of the Cappadocians, as we have mentioned above, was joined in a second marriage to Juba, king of Libya. When Juba died, she returned to her father. On seeing her there, Archelaus—thinking that, as her husband’s brother and her children’s uncle, he could hardly be shunned consistently with family devotion—began to love her so desperately that he cast out his wife Mariamme and put Glaphyra in her place. Not long afterwards, when the woman had returned to Judaea, she saw Alexander in a dream and wished to embrace him. But he seemed to withdraw from her embrace like an indignant man and to say: “Is this, Glaphyra, faithfulness to your promise? Is this how you have preserved my love for you, which you ought to have remembered? But let it be so: as a very young woman you had not refused a second marriage. But even a third? Even your husband’s brother? Did the injury to me so delight you that you were not ashamed to return to my house married to a third husband? But I shall see to it that my dishonour, your pollution, does not last longer. Nor will the incestuous man long rejoice in his brother’s marriage.” The woman rose and told her household the dream. By dying herself two days later, she confirmed that marriages of this kind do not go unpunished either by the laws of the living or by the wishes of the dead.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.3.1] Archelaus himself also saw in a dream nine large, full ears of grain being devoured by oxen. When he inquired, an interpreter answered that the nine ears signified the nine years in which he had enjoyed the fullest and greatest power. In the ninth year of his rule, therefore, a change would come upon him, since oxen, which were accustomed to turn the fields with the plough, signified a laborious change that would devour and swallow up his former achievements. On the fifth day after he learnt this, a man came from Caesar to take him to Rome for judgement. Condemned there and driven into exile, he fulfilled his dreams also in death.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.3.2] The dominion over the nation that had belonged to Archelaus was given the name of a province. This was the name the Romans gave to regions situated far away when they brought them under their authority by conquest. Yet the tetrarchs remained as before, Philip and Herod, the latter having changed the name by which he had previously been called, Antipas. For Salome, at her death, had left the places she held and authority over her people to Livia, Caesar’s wife. Such was the state of Judaea when Caesar died, leaving as successor to the rule of Rome his stepson Tiberius, the son of his wife Livia by an earlier husband. In his honour Herod founded Tiberias. Philip too thought that a city should be called Livia after the name of Tiberius’s mother.

The people were stirred to resist, and since he held that the images must be admitted, he drove very many to their deaths.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.3.4] While these events were taking place in Judaea, Agrippa, the son of Aristobulus, came to Rome, wishing to contest his case against Herod the tetrarch in a hearing before Tiberius. But, spurned by Tiberius, he remained at Rome and won very many friends, especially Gaius, Germanicus’s son. Whether he thought Gaius dear to the people through the favour attached to his father’s name, or closest to imperial power through his connection with the royal family, or acted from some foreknowledge, he cultivated him more eagerly than either his age or his rank warranted. Thus one day he raised his hands and prayed that Tiberius might die sooner and that he might see Gaius as emperor. When this was disclosed by his freedman Eutychus, Agrippa was led into chains at Tiberius’s command and cruelly tortured. He was not released before Tiberius ended his days. Yet Tiberius’s reign, foul with outrages, and his retreat on Capri, intolerable in its indolence, roused no man capable of effective action to kill him—because, I think, of reverence for the recently established rule of Rome, or of terror at his most savage cruelty, since harshness is very often safer the more oppressive it is.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.4.1] During his reign, the notorious outrage against Paulina, a woman of a most distinguished family, became widely known at Rome. She had an outstanding reputation for chastity among everyone, and was of surpassing beauty and eminent charm. Though assailed by the solicitations of Mundus, a commander of cavalry, she did not yield; but through the fault of excessive superstition she laid herself open to deception. The priests of Isis were suborned to bring her what purported to be a message from Anubis: he invited her to the temple, and, delighted by her devotion and chastity, asked for a night, having something he wished to entrust to her in secret. On receiving this, she joyfully reported to her husband that the god favoured her prayers, that the god asked for her presence, and that she could not refuse obedience. So, with both her own and her husband’s approval, she went to the temple of Isis and spent the night there. With witnesses removed far away, she lay down on her bed as though about to receive knowledge of a sacred mystery, thinking that her god would come to her in sleep and reveal himself to her in a vision. But when some of the night had passed, so that the woman could more easily be deceived while sound asleep, Mundus came in the face and dress of Anubis, lifted her clothes and rushed to kiss her. When she awoke, he told her that he was Anubis and displayed the face of Anubis. She believed him to be the god and declared herself blessed because her lord and god had deigned to visit her. She did not refuse when he sought her embrace, but asked whether a god could mate with a human being. He brought out examples: Alcmena had received Jupiter, the highest of the gods; Leda had enjoyed intercourse with him, as had very many other women who had given birth to gods. He also persuaded the woman that a god would be born of himself and her, and had intercourse with her. She returned to her husband happier still, saying that she, a woman, had mated with a god and, according to his promise, would bear a god. Her husband felt immense joy at the woman’s violation. Afterwards Mundus met the woman and said: “Paulina, blessed in your intercourse with a god! Great is the god Anubis, whose mysteries you have received. But learn not to refuse human beings any more than gods: the gods grant them what you have denied, since they do not disdain to give us either their forms or their names. See, the god Anubis called Mundus too to his rites, to join him to you. What good did your harshness do you, except to cheat you of the gain of the twenty thousand I had offered? Imitate the more indulgent gods, who grant us without payment what we could not obtain from you at a great price. But if human names offend you, it pleased me to be called Anubis, and the favour attached to this name helped to bring about the result.” Stunned by his words, the woman understood that she had been deceived. Grieving at the injury to her chastity, she confessed the deceit to her husband. He had no grounds for anger against his wife, to whom he had himself given permission to sleep in the temple, and, knowing her marital chastity, he brought a complaint before the emperor. Moved by the dishonour done to a powerful man and by the contrivance of an atrocious crime, the emperor dragged the priests from the temple, subjected them to torture and, after they confessed, killed them. He sank the statue of Isis in the Tiber. Mundus was allowed to flee, because, overcome by the force of love and the charm of beauty, he was thought deserving of a lighter penalty for his deeds.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.5.1] I therefore thought that I should not pass over the outrage that occurred while Tiberius ruled, so that the emperor’s depravity might be inferred from it. For just as a good ruler’s life is a kind of rule of probity and a pattern of living for everyone, so an emperor’s filth is a law of crimes. Pilate, sent by him to Judaea, a wicked man who made little of lying, deceived the Samaritans into going to the mountain named Gadir, which was sacred to them, on the claim that he wished to learn their mysteries. Going up, he forestalled the people with cavalry and infantry and struck them down on the fabricated charge that they had prepared to revolt from the Romans and seek a meeting place of their own.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.5.2] For what would he not dare, who had even nailed to a cross Christ the Lord, coming for the salvation of the human race, pouring out upon human beings the grace of his mercy through many divine works, and teaching nothing except what would make peoples obedient first to God and then to emperors? Madman, to be the minister of sacrilegious fury and kill the author of salvation! From that time, therefore, the fortunes of the Jews were ruined; from that time destruction was hastened for the nation and ruin for the temple. For if Herod, who delivered John to death, paid the price of his faithlessness and cruelty by being cast down from his kingdom and given over to exile, how much more must we understand the man who killed Christ to have been driven by headlong furies?

paragraphs.rawText: [II.5.3] I shall briefly explain the cause of John’s death. We have shown above that Philip and Herod, who was previously called Antipas, were brothers; Philip’s wife was Herodias, whom Herod joined to himself by an unlawful and unspeakable bond of marriage. John did not tolerate this and said to him: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” Then Herod, angered, thrust John into prison. Not long afterwards he killed this just man, a steadfast enforcer of divine law. For John had rebuked the incest of a brother’s bed not only as a preacher of the gospel, but also, as an enforcer of the law, had condemned the transgressor of the law who had taken away his living brother’s wife, especially when she had offspring by that same brother. Hence arose the hatred of almost all the Jews against Herod, and his punishment was hastened.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.5.4] Herodias brought this about. Seeing that Agrippa had become very influential with Caesar, she compelled Herod to go to Rome to win the emperor’s favour, taunting him with the disgrace of idleness: by shunning exertion and lingering at home, he allowed men unworthy of comparison with himself to be preferred to him. Since Agrippa had been made king from private station, how much less would Caesar hesitate to confer kingship upon him, who had long been a tetrarch! Unable to bear the woman’s reproaches, he therefore set out for Rome. While seeking Gaius’s friendship, he was accused by Agrippa and lost even the tetrarchy he had received from Julius Augustus. Fleeing to Spain with his wife Herodias, he was consumed by grief of mind.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.5.5] On Tiberius’s death, Gaius succeeded him. Wishing to be regarded and called lord and god, he gave the Jews grounds for most grievous sedition; had his rule not come to an early end, he would have brought the Jewish nation to an earlier end. For not only did he fail to restrain his own men from unlawful acts, but he even threatened those sent to Judaea with the ultimate punishment unless they carried out by arms every act against the law and sanctity of religion. Agrippa was very powerful during his rule, but, wishing to enclose Jerusalem with a very great wall so that the Romans could not take it—for he foresaw the impending ruin—he was overtaken by death and left the work unfinished.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.5.6] He exercised no less power under Claudius, since he had also taken part in the beginnings of his rule. When Gaius had been killed and Claudius himself had been raised to imperial power by the soldiers, the senate resisted him out of weariness with kingship. He sent Agrippa as an envoy, through whose mediation a pledge of moderation was given, goodwill established and peace agreed. In place of Agrippa the father, his son Agrippa was appointed king by Claudius Caesar.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.6.1] Won over by the persuasions of his wife Agrippina, Claudius himself too, as he was dying after thirteen years, appointed Nero emperor over the Roman dominion. Her deceit proved so powerful that she deprived the emperor’s son Britannicus, designated successor by the very right of nature, of any share in imperial power. She soon repented of this cunning: in providing for her own son, she had denied the emperor his, unaware that, exalted by power, her son would not even acknowledge his mother and would turn the reward for her benefit into her destruction. Yet he was married to Claudius’s daughter Octavia, a son-in-law preferred to a son in a reversal of the proper order, because the evils of the commonwealth weighed more heavily. It deserved a murderer of kin, a sacrilegious, incestuous man, so that crimes, not the merits of any good pursuit, should reign in him.

Eleazar, the chief of the brigands, had ravaged them most grievously for twenty years. At last, however, he was captured by Felix, who governed Judaea, and sent to Rome, where he paid a heavy penalty.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.6.3] Not even so was the people inhabiting Judaea broken by the great number of the slain. In Jerusalem itself another kind of brigand sprang up, called Sicarii. No longer hidden in secluded places or lying in wait in the darkness of night for travellers without protection, they struck in daylight, in the middle of the city and the press of the crowd, at anyone whom they approached. Carrying short swords in their hands and mingling with the crowded people, they stabbed someone beside them, and the unsuspecting victim fell with an unseen wound, death forestalling his cry. The corpse was in plain sight, but the killer was hidden. Anyone moved by another’s wound was brought nearer to his own and became one of the slain. Thus, whether through fear of danger or concealment of the crime, the Sicarius was not caught: such was the speed of those lying in wait and their skill in concealment. The priest Jonathan was killed; many were added each day. The fear of the living was heavier than the misery of the slain. Each day everyone went out as though to battle, but under a harsher condition: an enemy can be seen beforehand, whereas the Sicarius lurked unseen. Death was before their eyes, fear in their minds. No one believed that he would return, and not even friends were trusted while the Sicarius was feared.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.6.4] Terrified by this, many made for the desert. They were indeed innocent of the crime of brigandage or association with the Sicarii; their hands were innocent, but their judgement was weaker. Yet, while looking to their own interests, they aroused a fear of revolt, from which first suspicion of war against the Romans, and then odium, flared up. Moved by this, the ruler of the province sent cavalry and infantry and slaughtered a very great multitude.

He attached about thirty thousand Jews to himself and gathered them at the Mount of Olives. In repeated assaults he penetrated Jerusalem, even attacking the Roman guards who were stationed there to prevent any disturbance by the people.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.8.1] Finally, in the city of Caesarea, grave sedition arose between Jews and gentiles. The Jews claimed possession of the whole city on the grounds that it had been founded by Herod, a Jew. The gentiles resisted: its founder had indeed been a Jew, but he had given it Caesar’s name; moreover, he had built temples within it and set up statues, and so it seemed to have been assigned rather to gentile uses. The sedition arising from these disputes turned to blows, because the leaders of the Jews could not restrain their own people who were bent on sedition, and the gentiles thought it a disgrace to concede that they must yield to the Jews. They therefore roused Felix; as he sought to suppress the unyielding crowds on both sides, recourse was had chiefly to arms, since no other remedy was possible.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.8.2] Festus succeeded him and, after capturing very many brigands, delivered no small number to death. Albinus too, entrusted by the Romans with the same power, left no kind of wickedness untried. He was a wicked plunderer: anyone who had not given money was dragged into chains, though innocent; anyone who had given it was acquitted, even if guilty. Greed bred pride, so that he showed himself a tyrant to the poorer and a slave to the richer.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.9.1] “Although in many cases heedless grief, intolerant of counsel and restraint, makes some seethe with bitter complaints, when counsel is taken the feeling of grief is set aside. For if I had found all this people ready to avenge their injuries and make war upon the Roman dominion, and had not found the better and calmer part minded to choose peace and prefer quiet, I would not have dared either to come to you or to offer counsel. It is pointless to advise what ought to be done when the listeners favour the worse course. But some have no experience of the evils of war; others have a superficial hope of freedom, very sweet to seek but often unreasonable to expect to obtain—for many, in seeking freedom, heap up slavery, and everything is often snatched away from those who had at least the name of freedom left. Others, dissatisfied with their present circumstances because of their low standing, are attracted by change, and disturbance is reckoned a gain. I therefore thought I should deliberate with you, so that the sobriety of the more prudent should not be overborne by the audacity of the more insolent, or so that those who do not know how to judge rightly might at least learn from my admonition that they must yield to wiser counsellors. I therefore think you should grant me silence, so that I may set out what I believe is to your advantage, and that none of you should raise a disturbance if he hears anything against his wishes. For no one can judge the nature of what is said unless he has first heard it. Since he himself will decide whether to approve or reject it, he pointlessly raises a disturbance to avoid hearing it. Even after deliberation, each is free to hold the opinion he holds and, if he chooses to dissent, to maintain his ill-considered resolve even after sober warnings. But someone asks why I should wish to be heard in vain if those who hear me will not agree. Because, if they refuse to agree when they have heard, only part of my audience, not the whole people, will be endangered; but if they refuse to hear, even when only part of the audience raises a disturbance, the whole people is deprived of the benefit of hearing. My speech will therefore die even for those who wish to hear, if silence is denied me in any part of the assembly. For the whole speech is cut off and falls, as it were, lifeless, when the uproar of the assembly and its restless noise obstruct and kill it. There are therefore two things to which I think I must first reply, which carry the greatest weight in the complaints: that many cry out about the injuries inflicted by governors, and that many lament the loss of their freedom. These propositions seem to me to have been joined together and need to be separated. For if the governors are wicked, what need is there to raise the cry of freedom? You must not seem to accuse the governors as agents of domination out of loathing for slavery, rather than because they deserve it. Or, if slavery is intolerable, the complaint about the governors is needless. For even if they show restraint, slavery is still shameful. Let us therefore consider whether each of these provides substantial grounds for war. What is more foolish than to complain of injuries and weave a war out of them, exchanging insults for dangers, fleeing a judge and bringing in an enemy, when an unjust judge is often an interpreter of the law, whereas even a just enemy always seeks your life? A judge should therefore be soothed, not exasperated; an enemy should be avoided. Do not embitter the one and summon the other, since the one becomes gentler through soothing, while the other must be avoided so that he cannot harm you. In dealing with judges, then, take care that the complaint is not greater than the injury, and the odium of the charges heavier than the price of the offences. For often those who at first offended with some restraint become more insolent when accused, and those who previously stole in secret afterwards practise brigandage openly. Nothing so aggravates the heat of a wound as impatience in bearing it. Indeed, even with wild beasts, the tightest bonds press into them if they struggle and loosen if they remain still; and the severe force of fevers is lessened by endurance and increased by restlessness. If wild creatures know how to look to their own interests, forgetting their nature to relieve their pain, how much more has repeated experience taught human beings that the endurance of the injured has put those who injured them to shame, so that without an accuser they corrected what they would not have amended under accusation! But let it be granted that the insolence of Roman judges has been intolerable: which, then, is more tolerable, to endure them all or one? And what justice is there in making war upon all when one has injured you? Are all the Romans responsible for the injury? Is Caesar himself? Or was a wicked man deliberately chosen to be sent to you? They cannot keep watch across the seas and direct their eyes from west to east, to see there what is being done here, nor can they readily hear it: even if their concern demands it, distance denies it through the difficulty of obtaining evidence. Will one man’s guilt, then, tear the Roman world apart, when redress is swift even without your complaints, with none of the odium of an accusation and none of the toil of a journey? If you wish to flee them because you cannot overcome them, you must leave the world. But you put forward your desire for freedom. That deliberation comes late. You should have fought to avoid losing freedom, rather than to demand it back once lost. The experience of slavery is harsh; therefore either it should not have been accepted at the outset, or, once accepted, it must be borne calmly. The proper time to resist was when you were being summoned to servitude. That was the more just struggle. But anyone who has once given himself into slavery, even if he later wishes to withdraw, is not defended as a lover of freedom but condemned as a disobedient slave. Where was this defence of freedom when Pompey invaded your regions and entered the city as its lord? Where were the arms for freedom? Why were they laid down by our fathers? They were certainly stronger than we are. They were vigorous in spirit, abundant in resources, eager to resist, but they could not withstand a small portion of the Roman army. They were conquered but spared. They acknowledged the yoke of slavery so as not to endure the punishment of captivity. Why do you, their heirs, refuse what you owe by right of succession? Your fathers’ dealings bind you. How do you shun obedience when you are so much inferior to those who obeyed? Or what will remain for you when you rouse Caesar and all Roman strength against yourselves? How can you withstand those who have triumphed over all and are now helped by all who serve in their armies? The Athenians, for the freedom of all Greece, gave their homeland to the flames, exchanging their homes for exile so that Xerxes should not rule them. He sailed on land and walked upon the waves; neither the seas could contain him nor the land bear him, since his march encompassed the whole expanse of Europe, and the bounds of the lands were narrower than the passage of his army. The Lacedaemonians too, after Thermopylae and the triumphs of the dead Leonidas, after Agesilaus the explorer of Asia, now love their masters. Wherever you go, danger will follow you; indeed, you will find it there. For all are friends of the Romans, and whoever is outside Roman friendship is the enemy of all. Let love of your homeland enter your minds. If regard for your children and your wives does not restrain you, let the sight of the most sacred temple restrain you. Spare religion at least; spare the most holy priests, whom the Romans will no longer spare, nor the temple itself. They regret having spared them, since all nations have long wished to extinguish our religion; yet Pompey, though he could have extinguished it, spared it. I have omitted nothing; I have given every warning that concerns your safety. I advise you to take the course I choose for myself; consider what is to your advantage. I desire peace with the Roman people for you and for myself. If you refuse, you yourselves deprive yourselves of my alliance. Either we shall share favour, or you shall face danger without me.”

Others, dissatisfied with their present circumstances because of their low standing, are attracted by change, and disturbance is reckoned a gain. For no one can judge the nature of what is said unless he has first heard it. Since he himself will decide whether to approve or reject it, he pointlessly raises a disturbance to avoid hearing it. Even after deliberation, each is free to hold the opinion he holds and, if he chooses to dissent, to maintain his ill-considered resolve even after sober warnings. But someone asks why I should wish to be heard in vain if those who hear me will not agree. How did we become captives of the Assyrians? Did Scripture not say that these things would happen? Was it not written that all the sacred mysteries of the temple would be profaned? Now repeatedly profaned, they no longer manifest their power and the full grace of the mysteries. The temple has been defiled with human blood, the shrines filled with corpses, the altars drenched with gore. Battle has been fought on the Sabbath; transgression has been committed, since the temple is defended not by its own observance and the solemn keeping of holy days, but by bloody battle. And this, indeed, it says again. How, then, can we merit divine aid as though against enemies hostile to religion, when we ourselves transgress against our own religion? What remedy is there, then, when neither human resources support us nor divine grace comes to our aid? One or the other of these commonly invites people to war; you lack both. What therefore remains but manifest destruction? If you do not turn aside from it while there is still time to take care, you yourselves will do nothing but burn your homeland, set fire to the temple, and give your wives and children over to death. You will be responsible for their utter loss, when the inconsolable addition to all evils is that what we suffer should be ascribed to our own fault. Moreover, other cities’ wars end with the destruction of their own inhabitants; your rebellion will destroy the whole religion, which, spread throughout the world, has scattered its people everywhere, and in every city there is a portion of us. All Jews will therefore be involved in your battle, and there will be no region free of our blood. Or, if the Romans are such that they do not persecute Jews even when provoked by war, how unjust it is to make war upon those whose humanity you may hope for! It is good, dearest friends, it is good, while the ship is still in harbour, to foresee the coming storm. Let no one expose himself to imminent dangers, lest, once you have put out into the deep, you can no longer avoid shipwreck. Often, indeed, a storm arises suddenly, and war is encountered even if it is not begun; but there is a difference between provoking an enemy and receiving his attack. He spares more readily when unprovoked, and necessity excuses insolence; but when someone plunges into sheer danger, he is also burdened with reproach. This is not an enemy you can avoid by flight. Wherever you go, danger will follow you; indeed, you will find it there. For all are friends of the Romans, and whoever is outside Roman friendship is the enemy of all. Let love of your homeland enter your minds. If regard for your children and your wives does not restrain you, let the sight of the most sacred temple restrain you. Spare religion at least; spare the most holy priests, whom the Romans will no longer spare, nor the temple itself. They regret having spared them, since all nations have long wished to extinguish our religion; yet Pompey, though he could have extinguished it, spared it. I have omitted nothing; I have given every warning that concerns your safety. I advise you to take the course I choose for myself; consider what is to your advantage. I desire peace with the Roman people for you and for myself. If you refuse, you yourselves deprive yourselves of my alliance. Either we shall share favour, or you shall face danger without me.”

paragraphs.rawText: [II.9.2] As he said these things he wept, and so did his sister Berenice, for she too was in the upper part of the Xystus. Agrippa had moved them greatly with his tears, so that the Jews said: “We are not rebelling against the Romans, but think that war must be waged against Florus, who has done things that deserve war.” Agrippa answered: “But this is to make war upon the Romans; your deeds aim at injuring the Romans. Tribute is being withheld from the Romans, not Florus; from Caesar, not Florus. The soldier in the fortress called Antonia belongs to the Romans, not Florus. You have separated the temple from that fortress by demolishing and cutting off the porticoes, so that the guard should be kept apart. Restore the former state. Let the tribute owed to Caesar be paid to Caesar, lest Florus report that you have repudiated Caesar’s rule, not himself.”

paragraphs.rawText: [II.9.3] The people had agreed to these words: they went up to the temple with Agrippa, began to rebuild the porticoes as they had been, and collected the tribute. Industrious agents were sent for this task, and in a short time the forty talents lacking from the tribute payment were gathered. All the tumult of war had been suppressed, but Agrippa wished to add that they should obey Florus until a successor came to him from Caesar. He so exasperated the people that they did not refrain even from insulting him; when he was driven from the city, it is uncertain whether some struck him with stones they threw. Moved by this injury, the king had those responsible among them arrested and sent them to Florus. He himself withdrew to his kingdom.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.10.1] On his departure, the instigators of war laid an ambush and occupied the fortress of Masada, killing the Roman guards and installing their own. Eleazar too, the son of the chief priest, a man of reckless audacity, urged that no gift or sacrifice from any foreigner should be accepted. This was the trumpet of war against the Romans and roused everyone to tumult.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.10.2] All the leading men, therefore, seeing that this would cause a reckless revolt, argued with the people that not only was war being brought upon Caesar, but the institutions of religion were also being violated and reverence for the temple diminished. The traditions of the fathers, who had adorned the temple with foreigners’ gifts, were being arraigned and condemned. Its wealth had increased far more through the contributions of the nations and the gifts of diverse and innumerable nations. The ancestors’ sacred practices were being obliterated, the sacred rites changed. What would become of the things already given, if gifts from the nations were forbidden to be offered in the same way in future? Or, if the Romans alone were forbidden what everyone else was allowed, what an incitement to war this would be! Lastly, it was impious if only among the Jews were foreigners permitted neither to sacrifice nor to bring gifts. They ought to consider that Caesar’s peace would be broken. Offended by such a disturbance, he would undoubtedly deprive the Jews of all practice of sacrifice, so that those who had rejected Caesar’s sacrifice would not even sacrifice for themselves. This must be forestalled promptly: if such decisions reached Florus, and thence undoubtedly Caesar, they would bring ruin upon the Jewish nation.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.10.3] At the same time, wishing to support these points with the testimony of the priests, they asked whether a sacrifice of the gentiles had ever been rejected by their ancestors. Those bent on sedition raised an uproar to prevent this; not even the attendants dared to intervene in so great a dispute among the contending parties. Only one remedy seemed to remain: that Florus and King Agrippa should come with a military force, so that at least fear might make those desist whom counsel could by no means dissuade. But Florus wished the sedition to increase, so that there would be no room for pardoning the Jews: if they were caught up in war, all opportunity for them to press charges over his plunder and grave offences would be extinguished. He allowed the frenzy of war to grow and gave the envoys no reply. Agrippa, whom the embassy of his kinsmen Cylus, Antipas and Costobarus entreated most earnestly, was benevolent towards all. To preserve the Jews for the Romans, religion for the Jews, the temple for his homeland, the city for its citizens, and for himself the honour of rule and the tranquillity of his kingdom, he sent three thousand cavalry, with Darius and Philip as commanders of the squadrons, so that the advocates of the good cause, relying on this assistance, might exert themselves more readily.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.10.4] From this confidence arose among the good and indignation among the wicked. War grew: one side was stirred by a juster cause, which nevertheless gave no help in armed conflict, the other by frenzy and the size of its multitude. The fighters’ battle lines were divided. The chief priests and the portion of the people that desired peace, together with the royal cavalry, occupied the upper part of the city; the others, stationed in the lower parts, claimed for themselves the temple and the places near the sacred precincts. At first they provoked war on both sides with stones, rocks and volleys of missiles, and fought with arrows; afterwards, when the need for combat happened to arise, they came to grips. The royal troops excelled in skill and experience and wished to keep the instigators of war from approaching, lest they defile the temple. Eleazar and his men, by contrast, were intent on invading even the upper city, which was called Zion. Battle was fought for seven days without any interruption.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.10.5] The eighth day—a festival day on which everyone was accustomed to lay wood on the altars so that the fire should never fail, since it had to remain unextinguished—increased their frenzy, so that all the attendants were excluded from the temple. As the Sicarii rushed forward more boldly than usual, the royal troops yielded and did not dare to hold their ground even in the upper parts. The houses of Agrippa and Berenice were burned and all the royal furnishings plundered. Fire was carried around, so that even the debt notes stored in the public archives were burned, so that the poor might rise more insolently against their moneylenders. Thinking themselves released from every bond, they set fire to the city with their own hands. The sinews of the city were burned away. The fortress called Antonia was stormed, all the guards found there were killed, and it was afterwards burned.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.10.6] Menahem, son of Judas the Galilean, also hastened to Masada. An acute sophist, practised in unsettling affairs, he seized the armouries and armed the unarmed. Returning to Jerusalem with bodyguards attending him in royal fashion, he had become so immensely insolent that, rising above private station, he thought he need not refrain even from unlawful acts that free peoples could not endure. Many rose against him, denouncing him as a tyrant and master who, supported by royal attire, had weighed upon the citizens’ freedom. He paid a heavy penalty: tortured first, he died under his torments. Yet war was not removed, for a much graver disturbance arose.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.10.7] Finally, Metilius and the Roman soldiers begged leave to depart. A pledge of faith was given and oaths were sworn. When they had laid down their arms according to the agreement and were departing without fear, Eleazar and the members of his faction slaughtered them unavenged. The Roman soldiers thought they should neither resist force nor beg, but cried out only against the violation of faith and the perjury of the faithless. All were therefore killed; Metilius himself, the prefect of the soldiers, alone was spared by pleading and supplication, at the same time promising to become a Jew even to the point of circumcision.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.11.1] All Judaea was in flames, and the whole province of Syria too was roused to war. The people of Caesarea killed all the Jews they had among them. Roused by this grief, the Jews attacked very many cities of Syria and rose in revolt. Nowhere was there law, nowhere religion; the man who had plundered more was more highly honoured, as though piling up rewards of valour. It was a pitiable spectacle: unburied bodies lay everywhere in the cities, old men mingled with children, women too, without even coverings left to hide their private parts out of regard for the onlookers’ sense of shame. Everything was foul and full of pitiable sights. Although these grievous and wicked cruelties went beyond ghastly horror, they nevertheless threatened one another with still worse. There was monstrous brigandage between Jews and Syrians, since there was no hope of safety unless they forestalled one another. For what city did not contain Jews and Syrians mingled together? Days were passed in blood, nights in fear; neither hatred nor greed had any limit. For besides the differences of sect and worship, which had erupted into a public calamity so that each side wished the other destroyed, greed for possessions and the desire to plunder had seized their minds. They thought that no one should be spared whom they had assigned to death in their pursuit of plunder.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.11.2] Why speak of smaller numbers of the slain? For, apart from the people of Antioch, Sidon and Apamea, scarcely any people failed to persecute the Jews living among them. The people of Gerasa, however, even escorted those who wished to leave as far as their own borders, so that they might depart without any treachery.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.11.3] At Alexandria, however, a dispute arose between gentiles and Jews. When the Hebrews demanded vengeance and, seizing torches, threatened to burn the gentile people gathered in the amphitheatre, they drew the attention of Alexander Tiberius, the prefect of the place, who was occupied with other concerns, towards themselves. At first, indeed, he tried to restore public concord with peaceful words.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.11.4] But when he perceived that they mocked his earnest warnings and that so great a sedition could not be removed in any other way, he gave the soldiers permission to attack them. Attacking those crowded around, they made a very great slaughter throughout the city, killing some as they resisted, others as they hid in their houses. No pity for small children, no reverence for the aged, no regard for women came over them. Fifty thousand Jews were therefore killed. The streets swam in blood; everything was filled with corpses. Flames crackled in a savage fire throughout the city: kindled in the Jews’ houses, they also devoured the neighbouring buildings. At last Alexander relented and ordered the soldiers to desist and sound the retreat, but the mob’s anger, once it had gained the power to kill, was by no means assuaged.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.12.1] For they were paying the penalties for their own crimes: after crucifying Jesus, the arbiter of divine things, they went on to persecute his disciples. Yet many Jews and very many gentiles believed in him, drawn by his moral precepts and by an outpouring of works beyond human capacity. For them not even his death put an end to faith or grace; rather, it increased their devotion. They therefore laid murderous hands on their own kin and led the author of life to Pilate to be killed, and began to press the reluctant judge. Yet Pilate is not excused by this; the Jews’ madness is compounded, since he ought not to have condemned a man against whom he had found no guilt, nor ought they to have doubled their sacrilege with the murder of kin, so that the one who had offered himself to redeem and heal them was slaughtered by them. On this the Jews themselves also bear witness, since Josephus, the writer of histories, says that at that time there had been a wise man—“if indeed,” he says, “the creator of marvellous works ought to be called a man”—who had appeared alive to his disciples three days after his death, according to the writings of the prophets, who foretold both these and countless other things about him full of wonder. From him arose the congregation of Christians, and it spread into every race of humankind; no nation of the Roman world remained that had no share in his worship. If the Jews do not believe us, let them at least believe their own. Josephus said this, whom they themselves esteem the greatest; yet even in the very thing in which he spoke the truth, he was so errant in mind that he did not believe even his own words. He spoke for the sake of the faithfulness of his history, because he thought deception impious; he did not believe because of hardness of heart and obstinacy in faithlessness. Yet his failure to believe does not prejudice the truth; rather, it added more to the testimony, because, even unbelieving and unwilling, he did not deny it. In this the eternal power of Christ Jesus shone forth: even the leaders of the synagogue acknowledged as God the one they had seized for death. And indeed he spoke as God, making no exceptions for anyone and fearing no death, and announced that the temple too would be destroyed. Yet they were moved not by the injury to the temple but by his rebukes for their outrages and sacrileges. Hence their anger blazed up, so that they killed one such as no age had possessed. For while others had won by prayer the ability to do what they did, he had the power to command whatever he wished to be done.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.12.2] Before Jesus’ death, John the Baptist had been killed, a holy man who never held that true salvation lay in prosperity. Indeed, in addition to all the things full of righteousness that he taught, by which he invited the Jews to worship God, he had also instituted baptism for the purification of soul and body. His freedom of speech caused his death, because he could not endure Herod’s violation of his brother’s marriage rights and his taking his own brother’s wife away. For when this same Herod was going to Rome, he entered his brother’s house as a guest. His brother’s wife was Herodias, daughter of Aristobulus and sister of King Agrippa. Forgetful of nature, he dared to solicit her to leave his brother and marry him when he returned from the city of Rome; with the woman’s consent an incestuous compact was made. News of this affair reached King Aretas’s daughter, who was still married to Herod. Indignant at a rival, she conveyed to her husband on his return her wish to be sent to the town of Machaerus, on the frontier between the Petraean king and Herod. He suspected nothing. Moreover, since all his affection for her had already waned, he agreed to her departure, so that he might more easily keep faith with Herodias in their compact if he sent his wife away. But when she approached her father’s kingdom, she disclosed what she had learnt to her father Aretas. By an ambush he destroyed Herod’s whole army, which had been drawn into battle, through betrayal by those who had joined Herod from the people of Philip the tetrarch. Herod therefore brought his complaint to Caesar, but God’s indignation prevented the vengeance ordered by Caesar, for in the midst of the preparations for war Caesar’s death was reported. We find that the Jews judged and believed this, with Josephus as a competent authority against himself: Herod had lost his army not through human deceit but through God’s anger, and justly indeed, in vengeance for John the Baptist, a righteous man who had said to him, “It is not lawful for you to have that woman as your wife.”

paragraphs.rawText: [II.12.3] Yet we are weaving this account as though the Jews had kept lawful usages even among their own, when among them the right of the high priesthood had perished, destroyed either by greed or by the insolence of the more powerful, who thought that whatever they wished to do was lawful. For at the beginning Aaron was high priest, and in accordance with God’s will he transmitted the prerogative of the priesthood to his sons by lawful anointing. From them, in order of succession, were appointed those who held the primacy of the priesthood. Hence it became established by ancestral custom that no one should become chief priest unless he was of Aaron’s blood, since the right to this kind of priesthood had first been conferred upon him; a man of another lineage, even a king, could not lawfully succeed. Thus Uzziah, because he usurped the priestly office, was covered with leprosy and cast out of the temple, and spent the rest of his life without rule. He was certainly an excellent king, but he was not permitted to usurp religious office.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.13.1] From the fathers’ departure from Egypt to the building of the temple founded by Solomon there were therefore thirteen chief priests, amounting to six hundred and twelve years, since at first the man who was chief priest remained so until death and no one was substituted in the place of the living. Later men were appointed in their place even while they lived. These thirteen, then, obtained the priesthood by succession; in their times there were aristocracy, the monarchy of judges and the power of kings. Again, from Solomon to the time of the captivity, when the people migrated into Syria after the city was captured and the temple burned, there were eighteen chief priests over four hundred and sixty years, six months and ten days. The people were in captivity for seventy years. Afterwards Cyrus, when he released the people from the region of the Assyrians and gave them permission to build the temple, also allowed the chief priest Josedec, who had been carried away with them, to return, so that the observance of the old rite might be restored through an experienced priest’s knowledge. He himself and his successors, fifteen men in number, fulfilled the office in order of succession from the people’s return to Antiochus Eupator, and held the primacy of the priesthood for four hundred and fourteen years. Antiochus, whom we mentioned above, and his commander Lysias first appointed Jacimus to the priesthood in place of the chief priest Onias, whom they had killed. Although he was of Aaron’s line, he was not of that same house. Ananias, the brother of Onias, therefore went to Egypt and petitioned Ptolemy Philometor—who had introduced rites of observance modelled on the solemn worship at Jerusalem into the religious practices of the city of Alexandria—and Cleopatra, Philometor’s wife, to be appointed chief priest there, since Jacimus did not have the lawful succession to the priesthood. Both kingship and priesthood remained with Alexander until the last day of his life, for twenty-seven years, though often in an uncertain state: victory hung in the balance between him and Demetrius, and the citizens’ hatred was immense.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.13.2] As he was dying, Alexander saw that the hatred he had incurred would be a dangerous inheritance for his sons. He wished his wife Alexandra to take the helm of the kingdom: she was trained by experience of rule and the habit of shared counsel, yet more favoured by the people, because she had often protected those endangered by her husband’s cruelty and restrained her husband. At the same time he appointed her to decide which of his sons in particular should be entrusted with the high priesthood. She put Hyrcanus in his father’s place in the priesthood, either because of the prerogative of his greater age or because, being of a gentler disposition than his brother, he seemed unlikely to cause his mother any trouble over the affairs of the kingdom. She entrusted no public office to Aristobulus, but even while his mother lived he took advantage of her illness to play the king in remote and more strongly fortified places. Offended by this and anxious over Hyrcanus’s complaints, his mother aggravated her illness. Her rule lasted no more than nine years, and she left Hyrcanus heir to everything, not because she expected him to keep it, but so as not to help an unworthy man or encourage a usurper’s insolence by a more favourable judgement.

Defeated in war, he withdrew to more strongly fortified places and detained Aristobulus’s wife and children, whom he had found in the fortress. He welcomed a change of status: all power and the priesthood were to pass to Aristobulus, while he himself, as a private citizen, was to withdraw to Aristobulus’s house.

Then, when he saw that the Arab king’s assistance was weak against the Romans, whom Aristobulus had enticed into his alliance through Scaurus, he brought his complaint to Pompey as he approached.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.13.5] Aristobulus, now in the third year of his rule, was evading Pompey. Pompey assailed him in war, seized him by his authority and placed him under guard before victory. After overcoming his people and taking the city, he ordered Aristobulus himself to be sent captive to Rome with his sons, restored the dignity of the priesthood to Hyrcanus, and appointed him to preside over the citizens, but without a diadem or the insignia of kingship. He was generous in honour but concerned for quiet, lest peace be disturbed by the spirit of Aristobulus’s insolence. Thus Aristobulus, though captive, stripped Hyrcanus of kingship; Hyrcanus afterwards spent twenty-four years in power, greater in practice than in name.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.13.6] Yet the end of Hyrcanus’s power was not the end of his life. The rest of his life was spent in dishonour, as we mentioned above. Defeated in battle as the Parthians crossed the Euphrates, he was captured and put into the power of Antigonus, Aristobulus’s son. Even with his ears cut off, he had not yet endured the full bitterness of his pitiable suffering. For after these events he was also carried into exile in Parthia, a feeble old man who became a laughing-stock for the barbarians. Later, on learning that Herod ruled, to whom his granddaughter Mariamme was married, he returned to Judaea. There he was at first received with the greatest show of honour, so that a veil might be drawn over the plots; not long afterwards he was killed on the fabricated charge that he wished to regain power.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.13.7] Herod had thus obtained the kingdom, which he had received from the Romans as the reward for attacking or betraying his homeland. In the place of Antigonus, who had held power for three years and three months, he appointed successors to the priesthood, not men of the Hasmonean lineage, whom we have learnt to have been of more illustrious ancestry, but any obscure men whom his whim or chance offered. Yet, worn down by the entreaties of his mother-in-law Alexandra, or frightened by her accusations, he appointed Jonathan, his wife’s brother, a young man of seventeen, as priest. Soon he himself put him to death, suspecting him of seeking rule, because each day he saw immense favour for him growing among the whole people. Passing over Anhelus, whom he had already appointed to the priesthood from among the obscure before Jonathan, he then chose the rest in succession, men of such a kind that he had nothing to suspect of them. For how would he not guard against in strangers what he had been unable to endure in a relative by marriage? Archelaus followed similar practices in such appointments: under the guise of his father’s custom he maintained the outlook of a narrower mind, following a sort of habit innate in mortals, among whom the sluggishness of duller men arouses less suspicion than the favour enjoyed by good men. Yet a weak mind is more insolent in prosperity, while a wiser one knows how to repay benefits.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.13.8] Thus from Herod’s reign to Roman rule, which had added Judaea to the other provinces after Archelaus was deposed, and thence to the destruction of the temple and the triumph of Titus, there were twenty-eight chief priests over a hundred and seventy years. Most of them, indeed, only discharged the duties of the dignity; a few also held the right to exercise power. It is therefore clear that succession from the lawful lineage did not continue among the chief priests, for not all were descended from Aaron or from his sons, who were put in his place and left for the others the pattern of the prescribed succession. Thus, when the ancestors’ institutions had been corrupted by the greed or faithlessness of their own people, the laws of religion violated and the safeguards of antiquity torn apart, divine aid abandoned them not undeservedly. They were consequently assailed with every kind of injury as a people left defenceless: in domestic seditions they turned their hands against themselves, were afflicted by grievous brigandage, and received the vilest judges as their lot, so that men worse still succeeded the wicked.

Florus raised the torch of war and kindled battle between the Romans and the Jews, which caused the final destruction of the temple and the city.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.14.1] For when Cestius, who had received supreme military command in the regions of Syria from the Romans, learnt that the Jews were ablaze with the fury of war, he took up arms in the twelfth year of Nero’s reign to avenge the killing of the Roman soldiers who had been entrusted with the duty of restraining insolence and preserving peace. Having gathered the allies’ auxiliaries too, he entered Judaea. The inhabitants of the city named Zabulon had scattered in fear, leaving it full of riches which their owners had been unable to carry with them when they fled to the higher parts of the mountains. He allowed his army to plunder it. He also admired the beauty of its public works and ordered it to be burned.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.14.2] As though this were too little for vengeance, he sent his army ahead to prevent anyone from escaping destruction by flight and seized Joppa, the men he had sent breaking in by land and sea. Eight thousand men and nearly four hundred more were killed; once its spoils had been plundered, the city was burned. He also laid waste the country near Caesarea, plundered what he found and burned the villages.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.14.3] Sepphoris checked his onslaught, for all its inhabitants came out to meet Cestius. Soothed by their favour and goodwill, he left the city free from disaster. A band of brigands was active in these parts, but on the army’s arrival they had withdrawn to the mountains. They boldly attacked and harried Gallus, commander of the twelfth unit, as he advanced to battle, killing about two hundred Romans. But when the Romans occupied the higher ground, the brigands could not withstand the infantry at close quarters; as they fled, the cavalry easily surrounded and killed them. More than two thousand were therefore slain, and a few were put to flight who managed to hide in the steep parts of the mountains. The whole region was cleared of brigandage.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.14.4] Gallus returned to Caesarea; Cestius marched to Antipatris with his whole force. There the Jews had massed no small multitude. But before they joined battle, they scattered in different directions, leaving the countryside and villages to plunder and fire.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.14.5] Lydda too was found empty of inhabitants and burned. Gabao, which lay fifty stades from Jerusalem and was plainly visible, roused the Jews to arms when it received the Roman army. Disregarding the celebration of the Sabbath, which they solemnised with ancient worship and customary observance, they sprang upon the Romans with such force that they would have routed the whole army had the cavalry not come to the aid of the hard-pressed infantry. Five hundred and fifteen Romans were killed, but all had been in grave danger; twenty-two of the Jews were lost in battle. Here the valour of Monobazus and Cenedaeus shone forth. On learning that the Jews were rising against the Roman battle lines, they attacked from the front, drove back many and forced them to return to the city.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.15.2] King Agrippa, seeing that this could not be attempted without great slaughter on both sides, sent his men Borcius and Phoebus to tell the people that whatever outrage they had committed against the Romans could be pardoned, if only they would lay down their arms and take thought for their safety in future. He judged that he should either persuade them all to renounce battle or detach a portion from the rest. The rebels, by contrast, fearing that one or other of these aims might succeed, attacked the envoys and killed Phoebus; Borcius was wounded and barely managed to escape.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.15.3] Seeing disputes of this kind in the city, in which some rose against the envoys while others urged that the Romans should be received into the city, Cestius tried to force his way in. He drove those who resisted back as far as Jerusalem, and himself approached with his army to within three stades of the city. He spent three days there; on the fourth he attacked, entered Bethesda and immediately burned it, along with Caenopolis. As he pressed on towards the upper parts of the city and the rebels fled further inside, had he decided to force his way into the city, the whole war would undoubtedly have been ended.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.15.4] Indeed, Ananus son of Jonathan had stationed many men to call out invitations to the Romans as though they were about to open the gates. But while Cestius was either being held back by Priscus and many centurions, who had been bribed by Florus and wanted the war to grow, or placed too little trust in the invitation, Ananus and his men were driven from the wall. When they fled to their homes, the rebels occupied their position. For five days the Romans tried different approaches. When they saw that they could not force an entry, they selected the strongest men and the archers and attacked the temple from the northern side. The Jews were not idle either: they fought bravely and grew prouder as they repeatedly drove back the enemy. At last, however, some were wounded by the multitude of arrows, others struck and terrified, and they yielded to the Romans, who had begun to undermine the wall and set fire to the temple gate.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.15.5] Great fear had come upon the rebels, and a kind of bewilderment of mind. Many fled as though escaping the city’s imminent destruction. By not daring to stand their ground, they had given confidence to the people: with the departure of those whose multitude had hemmed them in, they now felt free and released from a sort of siege by the wicked. They poured around the gates to open them and receive Cestius as though he had come to defend the city, not to attack it. But Cestius himself was also suddenly seized by a kind of stupor, so that he noticed neither the desperation of the wicked nor the eagerness of the common people. Had he persisted a little longer in what he had begun, he would have put an end to the war and captured the city. But, as far as we are allowed to understand, God’s will, hostile to the Jews, postponed the imminent end of the war until ruin should engulf very many, indeed almost all, of the Jewish nation. The wait, I think, was for the enormity of their crimes to grow into every kind of wickedness and, with the increase of impiety, to reach the full measure of the worst outrages.

But Cestius himself was also suddenly seized by a kind of stupor, so that he noticed neither the desperation of the wicked nor the eagerness of the common people. Had he persisted a little longer in what he had begun, he would have put an end to the war and captured the city. But, as far as we are allowed to understand, God’s will, hostile to the Jews, postponed the imminent end of the war until ruin should engulf very many, indeed almost all, of the Jewish nation. The wait, I think, was for the enormity of their crimes to grow into every kind of wickedness and, with the increase of impiety, to reach the full measure of the worst outrages.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.15.6] How was it that, when he ought to have pressed hard, Cestius suddenly recalled his army and raised the siege? This sudden change of circumstances, contrary to expectation, broke the spirits of the good, while the brigands took heart and gained confidence. Turning from flight to pursuit, they attacked the rear of the column and slaughtered many cavalry and infantry there as they rushed about in confusion. The day was already declining. Cestius therefore feared the approach of night and the gloom of darkness, on which men who knew the country would rely all the more to press from every side upon those unfamiliar with the region. He built a rampart outside the city. On the following day, by withdrawing from the enemy, he roused them to arms against himself, so that they took fear to be the cause of his departure. Surrounding the Romans on the flanks and from behind, they killed the rearmost men and harassed the marching army with javelins. A mass of missiles hurled into closely packed ranks did not easily miss its mark. If anyone dared to strike back, he exposed himself to a wound; if anyone turned against his assailant, he was left by his own men and surrounded by the enemy. The pursuer is always better protected than the man ahead of him: the one covers his breast, while the other exposes his back to the enemy. Thus the Romans, who had come to besiege, were pressed hard as though themselves besieged. They could no longer hold out or endure. They were weighed down by their own arms, while the enemy were swifter and not easy to overtake; their greatest fear was that their line might be broken. Under these unequal conditions of combat they could not harm the enemy, although they themselves suffered grievously. Cestius hesitated, uncertain what to do, as he saw his men being worn down all along the route and many of his senior officers already stricken. He halted for two days, as though to restore the weary men. But he saw the number of the enemy growing more and more, the whole surrounding country full of adversaries, and his delay working against him because more were gathering. On the third day, seeking a quicker and easier passage, he ordered the column’s baggage to be removed.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.15.7] The beasts of burden were killed, most of the wagons smashed, and other things of this kind, which in danger were more a burden than a help, were destroyed or hurled down, including siege equipment and kinds of missiles. Such things caused them all the greater fear, lest they arm the enemy against themselves with their own resources. Many covered the sky with javelins and the column with arrows, never slackening in their task, while only their opponents suffered destruction. By now even the infantry could no longer hold out. A cliff on one side and precipices on the other denied them room either to flee or to defend themselves. The Jews, by contrast, were fired all the more by the hope of victory. They bore down on the weary, pressed those who were stuck and mocked those in despair. They would have destroyed almost all the forces of the Roman army had night not come to its aid, its darkness obstructing battle. The Romans spent the night at a nearby place named Bethoron, while the Jews surrounded them on every side and watched the exits to prevent the Romans from slipping away.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.15.8] Cestius, despairing of an open passage, tried to escape by deceit. He therefore selected forty men in whom despair of escape had instilled contempt for death. He stationed them in the fortifications and ordered them to carry out their watch duties throughout the night, making as much noise as possible around the rampart. No preparations for the army’s departure were to be revealed to the Jews by the usual signs through which men in confusion commonly betray themselves. All the rest were to leave in silence, while the Jews suspected nothing: hearing the customary noises of the guards, they would think that all the Romans remained in position. By this deception Cestius led out his army, and had already covered thirty stades, relying in uncertain circumstances on the faithfulness of a few. These men, facing death, preferred to make a free gift of their peril to their comrades rather than waste it. Night had concealed the deceit, but day revealed it. When the light spread, the situation became clear and the whole place where the Romans had been appeared empty. The Jews attacked first those whose pretended duties had deceived them. After killing the forty men with little difficulty, they pursued the army, which had covered a great distance during the night and pressed on still more quickly by day, lest it again become entangled in the dangers of night. The road was full of baggage which the fleeing Romans abandoned so that no one would be delayed beneath an excessive load. Vessels, utensils and even things necessary for war lay everywhere: ballistae, battering rams and the other equipment brought to destroy the city. The pursuing Jews passed them by lest they cause delay; on their return they gathered them to use against those who had abandoned them. They pursued as far as the city of Antipatris. When they found that the whole Roman army had passed beyond it and their hope of overtaking it had vanished, they turned back, gathered the spoils of the slain and returned to Jerusalem in triumph and with hymns. So great was their joy: with few of their own lost, five thousand three hundred infantry and three hundred and eighty cavalry of the Roman army had been killed. This took place in the twelfth year of Nero’s reign, as we mentioned above.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.16.1] But not all the Jews shared that exultation. After what had been not a battle for Cestius but a calamity, there were some who longed to rescue themselves as though from the ultimate danger of a sinking ship and swim clear of the city’s shipwreck. Foremost among them were the brothers Custobarus and Saul, with Philip, the commander of King Agrippa’s army. They fled to Cestius and asked to be sent to Nero in Achaea. Cestius welcomed them willingly and did not refuse their request, so that through them Caesar might be told that Florus had been the cause of the war; that he himself had undertaken a war of the utmost necessity; and that the army had been surrounded by an unexpected multitude of conspirators, though it was clear that the commander’s judgement had rescued it from danger rather than entangled it. They were to say that Cestius had tried to calm the hatred aroused against Florus but had been unable to do so, and had therefore encountered war, not begun it. These were their instructions: by arousing all Caesar’s indignation against Florus, he hoped to lessen Caesar’s displeasure with himself, which he greatly feared because he knew how badly events had been managed.
