paragraphs.rawText: [II.16.2] Many were so terrified by the defeat of the Roman army that the people of Damascus, fearing the taint of a suspected alliance because they shared a place of residence, killed the Jews who inhabited the city with them and had been gathered in the gymnasium. The Damascenes had arranged this long before, whether from suspicion or deceit: the Jews were to be separated from the gatherings of the gentiles, lest they attempt an uprising by night, or so that they alone would be exposed to destruction. It was all kept in the deepest secrecy, so that discussion of this undertaking should not reach even their own wives, since the women too, for the most part, participated in Jewish worship.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.17.1] They therefore attacked them all in the confined space and killed ten thousand Jews. It was easy for unarmed men, taken by surprise by armed men, to perish. A recent example of this savagery had gone still further at Scythopolis, and I think it incited the Damascenes. For when the Jews were laying waste all the neighbouring places, they came to Scythopolis. They tried to win over the Jews living there, but found enemies in those whom they had thought faithful to them, because, as is the way of human nature, concern for safety outweighed the bond of kinship among them. Putting fellowship with their tribe in second place, they preferred association with their fellow inhabitants and threatened their tribesmen with slaughter. This aroused the gentiles’ suspicion, for hostility against their own people was being displayed with such ready zeal. They feared that a trap was being prepared under a pretence, and that the Jews would attack the city by night when its inhabitants were less watchful, strike down all the gentiles and regain favour for themselves among the Jews. Therefore, if they wished to prove their faith even towards the gentiles, they were to leave the city with all their families and go to the neighbouring grove. When this was done, the people of Scythopolis remained quiet for two days so that the Jewish group would lay aside suspicion and assume a sense of safety. On the third night, when their trust in assumed goodwill had removed their concern to keep watch, force was brought against them while they were unsuspecting and asleep. Thirteen thousand people were killed, and everything they possessed was plundered.

paragraphs.rawText: [II.18.1] Simon’s suffering demands an account: bitter to see and pitiable to hear, yet memorable for the unusual nature of the event. He was one of the Jewish people, born of Saul, a father of no mean standing. Endowed with boldness of spirit and strength of body, he exercised both to destroy his own tribesmen. In repeated attacks he killed very many of the Jews who had come from elsewhere. If they happened to come against him in a united body, he was accustomed to withstand their battle line alone and drive back their massed ranks. He was the knot that held up the whole battle, and often brought a reversal when the situation was desperate. As a resident of Scythopolis he rendered this military service to his fellow citizens against his own people. But the vengeance owed to kindred blood was not long delayed. For when the people of Scythopolis broke faith, surrounded those who had gone to the grove by agreement and began to press and assail them in war, they destroyed the rest of the multitude and attacked even Simon’s children and parents, though from a distance, with missiles and weapons. Simon saw the countless multitude gaining an easy advantage, so that it could not be withstood much longer. He drew his sword, turned towards the enemy and cried out: “People of Scythopolis, I receive what my deeds deserve. By killing my kinsmen I testified to the goodwill I bestowed upon you, and I gave the blood of my brothers as a pledge of your favour, though faithlessness would more justly be ascribed to you. Now, by keeping faith with foreigners, I have failed to keep it with my own. I have also betrayed my children and parents; yet you ought not to have killed them, if you had considered the reward for my crime. I shall therefore die, angry with everyone, a friend to no one, since I have betrayed my own people; and with my own hands I shall first exact vengeance upon myself. I have killed the companions of my religion and those who shared my faith; I recognise the debt of my crime. I shall pay with a murder of kin worthy of so great a sacrilege, so that this may be both punishment for my outrage and glory for my valour, lest anyone else boast of wounding my family. Afterwards my right hand will turn against myself, so that my death may be seen to come from madness, not weakness. Let no one mock me as I fall. Let madness avenge the murder of kin, and the murder of kin avenge sacrilege.” Having said this, he turned his gaze upon his children and parents. With indignant eyes, as pity mingled with anger was already coming upon him, he seized his father from their midst and ran him through with his sword. After him his mother was dragged forward, so that there would be no one to intercede for her grandchildren. His wife willingly offered herself next, so that she would not survive the fall of so great a husband. His children came forward, lest in death itself they be judged unworthy of so great a father. He hastened to forestall the enemy with swift strokes. When he had killed his whole family, he stood amid the corpses of his own people, as though he had triumphed over his family affections because he had seen none of his own die by another’s sword. He raised his right hand so that everyone could see and, mastering the death that was terrible to all, ran himself through with his own sword as a victor. He was a memorable young man for his outstanding bodily strength and greatness of spirit; but because he gave his faith to foreigners rather than to his own people, he deserved such an end.Translation comparison: Pollard takes perfidia tribueretur as attributing faithlessness to the Scythopolitans. Millet instead makes Simon say that he would have been more justified in treating them treacherously: tribuere can concern attribution or the bestowal of treatment.
